questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A painter's own account of himself
questions.learningObjective: Set out what a painter's account of himself is worth
questions.stem: The clerk's file on a disputed painting contains a letter in which a painter described himself as the pupil of another and never once named a master of his own.

options.text: That the statement is a claim about his training, to be weighed like any other evidence.
That the painter had no master, since a man who names no teacher cannot have had one.
options.misconception: reads silence in a record as denial

options.text: That the letter is a forgery, since painters never wrote about their own training.
options.misconception: assumes a painter's words are evidence of nothing

options.text: That the painting is early, since a pupil's work must always be made before the master's career ended.
options.misconception: assumes a pupil's work is always earlier

questions.explanation: A painter's account of his own training is a statement made for his own purposes, so it is evidence to be weighed rather than a fact. Silence about other teachers proves nothing about dates.
questions.hint: Ask who the statement was made for.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Convincing ageing beside modern materials
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a patterned crack network
questions.stem: A second file note compares the panel's surface with a report from a laboratory and finds that the cracks run at regular intervals of about two millimetres across the whole picture.

options.text: That the cracking is patterned rather than natural, and the surface must be examined before it is dated.
That the panel is in excellent condition, since a fine crack pattern shows a well prepared ground.
options.misconception: reads a regular pattern as good condition

options.text: That the panel is a nineteenth-century pastiche, since old panels never crack in a regular line.
options.misconception: assumes a pattern proves a particular date

options.text: That the cracks are natural, since a picture in a dry room always cracks at even intervals.
options.misconception: assumes an even pattern must be natural

questions.explanation: Cracks at even spacing across a whole surface are characteristic of a deliberately applied pattern. That is a reason to examine the surface closely, not a date and not a verdict on the panel.
questions.hint: Ask what an even crack spacing suggests.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a school attribution says
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a school attribution asserts
questions.stem: The clerk's file asks what the phrase school of the workshop means in a disputed attribution, and the archivist answers in a short statement.

answer.exemplar: School of the workshop is a claim about training and method rather than about a person, and it says that the work was produced inside a group that shared a way of working. It does not name a hand, and it does not fix a date beyond the period in which that group was active, so a school attribution is a hypothesis about connection and not an identification.

questions.explanation: A school attribution claims a shared training and method rather than a named hand, and it bounds a work to the period the group was active. It is a claim about connection, not an identification.
questions.hint: Ask whether the phrase names a person.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A label that the handling contradicts
questions.learningObjective: Count the features that support an attribution
questions.stem: A technical report listed in the file examines twelve features of the handling of a panel and finds that five of them contradict the attribution in the label. How many of the features listed support the attribution?
questions.explanation: The report lists twelve features and five work against the attribution, so 12 minus 5 features agree with it. That is 7 supporting features, which have to be weighed one by one.
questions.hint: Subtract the contradicting features from the total.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a workshop contract records
questions.learningObjective: Say what a workshop contract settles

stimulus.body: A file note reproduces a contract of 1591 between a master painter and two assistants, which fixes the price at 240 florins, of which 60 is to pay for materials, and which names two altarpieces to be made for a chapel. A clause states that the assistants shall follow the master's design in every part.

questions.stem: A file note reproduces a workshop contract of 1591 between a master painter and two assistants, and the clerk is asked what the contract settles and what it leaves open.

options.text: That it settles price, materials, the number of pictures and the division of labour, but not the handling.
That it settles everything about the two altarpieces, since a contract cannot leave anything open.
options.misconception: assumes a contract leaves nothing open

options.text: That it proves the master painted both panels himself, since he agreed the design of every part.
options.misconception: reads a design clause as proof of the hand

options.text: That it fixes the date of the pictures, since a contract must be made in the year the work was finished.
options.misconception: assumes a contract dates the work

questions.explanation: A contract fixes the bargain: what is to be made, at what price, with what materials, and who does which part. It says nothing about the handling of the paint.
questions.hint: Ask what the document was drawn up to settle.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Patronage and the subject of a picture
questions.learningObjective: Separate a patron's terms from an artist's choices
questions.stem: The clerk's file asks about a picture commissioned by a guild for its own hall, and the archivist is asked to work in two stages: first to say what the patron asked for, and then to say what the painter chose.

options.text: Say what the guild asked for, then say what the painter added to it within the terms of the commission.
Say what the guild asked for, then say that the painter's own wishes did not matter to the result.
options.misconception: assumes a commission removes the artist's choice

options.text: Say what the guild asked for, then say that the subject shows what the guild most valued.
options.misconception: reads a subject as the patron's whole intention

options.text: Say what the guild asked for, then say that the guild's officers drew the design themselves.
options.misconception: assumes a patron designed the picture

questions.explanation: A commission sets the terms, including the subject, and within them the painter makes choices that belong to the work. The subject is one of the patron's conditions, not the whole intention.
questions.hint: Separate the terms given from the choices made.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A commission and its stated purpose
questions.learningObjective: State what a commission letter settles
questions.stem: A commission letter entered in the file states that the panel is to be carried in procession on a feast day each year, and the clerk asks what the letter settles.

options.text: The intended use of the panel, which is evidence about how it was made and where it was kept.
The name of the painter, since a commission letter is always written by the person who made the work.
options.misconception: assumes a letter's author is the painter

options.text: The value of the panel, since a commission states what the work was worth to the guild.
options.misconception: assumes a document fixes a market value

options.text: The date of the work, since a letter that mentions a feast day must be written in that year.
options.misconception: assumes a letter dates the work

questions.explanation: A commission letter records the terms, and the stated use tells a curator how the object was meant to be handled and kept. It does not name the painter, fix a price, or date the work.
questions.hint: Ask what the letter was written to record.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A painter's own account of himself
questions.learningObjective: Interpret conflicting statements in a self-account
questions.stem: A file note counts the statements a painter made about his own work: two claims that he painted from his own invention, one that he followed a design left by another, and one denial that a picture was his.

options.text: That the statements pull in different directions, so the account shows a reputation being managed.
That the two claims of invention are false, since a painter who denies a picture cannot also claim two.
options.misconception: assumes a painter's statements are consistent

options.text: That the denial proves the picture is not his, since an artist never gives up a work in writing.
options.misconception: reads a denial as a confession

options.text: That the following of a design means the picture is a copy, since invention and copying cannot meet.
options.misconception: assumes design and invention are exclusive

questions.explanation: A painter's statements that pull in different directions are part of how he presented his work, and that presentation is itself evidence. It is not a fixed record of any single picture.
questions.hint: Ask what a self-account is doing for its writer.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Convincing ageing beside modern materials
questions.learningObjective: Explain how an artificial ageing is produced
questions.stem: The clerk's file asks how a modern restorer can make a surface look three centuries old, and the archivist answers in a short statement.

answer.exemplar: Ageing a surface is a matter of imitating the marks that time leaves, and a restorer can lay in a fine crack pattern, darken the recesses and dull the high points so that the paint appears to have been handled and moved for three hundred years. The trouble is that the effect is a picture of age rather than age itself, and it sits on the surface where the evidence of the work ought to be.

questions.explanation: Ageing a surface imitates the marks of time, and a convincing imitation can cover the evidence a work carries. Surface appearance must therefore be checked against materials and handling.
questions.hint: Ask what the imitation stands in for.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a school attribution says
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the part of a group left unassigned
questions.stem: An attribution in the file names a school and then singles out three named hands within it, from a group of twenty-four works attributed to the school. How many of the twenty-four works are not assigned to a named hand?
questions.explanation: The group holds twenty-four works and three of them are assigned to named hands, so the rest number 24 minus 3. That is 21 works that the school attribution covers without identifying a hand for them.
questions.hint: Subtract the named hands' works from the group.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A label that the handling contradicts
questions.learningObjective: Weigh a handling comparison against a label

stimulus.body: A note in the file compares the handling of a panel signed with a famous name with the handling of three undisputed works by that painter. The panel's flesh tones are laid in wet, its shadows are transparent browns, and its highlights are small loaded strokes, while the undisputed works use layered glazes and blended transitions.

questions.stem: A note in the file compares the handling of a panel signed with a famous name with the handling of three undisputed works, and asks what the comparison establishes.

options.text: That the handling differs from the established manner, which is a serious objection to the signature.
That the panel is a copy, since no apprentice could work as well as the master.
options.misconception: assumes only a master could paint well

options.text: That the signature must be false, since a panel carrying it must match the painter's documented manner.
options.misconception: assumes a mismatch proves a false signature

options.text: That the panel is early, since painters always changed their manner when they were young.
options.misconception: assumes early work differs from later work

questions.explanation: A comparison with undisputed works that shows a different manner is a serious objection to an attribution and the start of further enquiry. It does not by itself prove a false signature or fix a date.
questions.hint: Ask what the comparison is evidence of.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a workshop contract records
questions.learningObjective: Read a payment as evidence of employment
questions.stem: Another note in the file asks about a contract that records a master's payment to an assistant, and the clerk is asked to work in two stages: first to say what the payment shows, and then to say what it does not show.

options.text: Show that the assistant was employed, then leave open which parts of a work each hand painted.
Show that the assistant was employed, then show that every part of the work was his to paint.
options.misconception: assumes employment fixes the hand

options.text: Show that the assistant was employed, then show that the master's paintings of that year are all his own.
options.misconception: assumes a payment settles a period's authorship

options.text: Show that the assistant was employed, then show that the contract was a partnership rather than a wage.
options.misconception: reads a payment as a partnership

questions.explanation: A payment shows that a person was employed and paid, and it is real evidence about how a workshop was staffed. It says nothing about which part of a particular panel each person painted.
questions.hint: Ask what a payment proves and what it leaves.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Patronage and the subject of a picture
questions.learningObjective: State what a commissioned subject shows
questions.stem: A file note sets out the terms of a commission for a picture of a battle, and the clerk asks what the note lets the file claim about the subject.

options.text: That the battle was the subject the patron asked for, making the picture a statement of that claim.
That the battle was the patron's own, since a guild only paid for pictures of its own history.
options.misconception: assumes a patron's choice is a literal claim

options.text: That the painter chose the battle, since a commission fixes the size and the price rather than the subject.
options.misconception: assumes a commission leaves the subject free

options.text: That the battle was invented, since painted battles were usually invented to flatter a family.
options.misconception: assumes a flattering subject is always false

questions.explanation: A commissioned subject is a choice the patron made and paid for, and that makes the picture a statement of the patron's claim. It does not follow that the event was the patron's own.
questions.hint: Ask who chose the subject and who paid for it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A commission and its stated purpose
questions.learningObjective: Identify an unsupported claim in a description
questions.stem: Two drafts of a commission description are compared in the file, and the first names the intended use and the subject, while the second adds that the picture was made to teach the viewer a lesson.

options.text: That the second draft adds a claim about the picture's effect that the commission itself does not support.
That the second draft is the better account, since a fuller description always helps a reader.
options.misconception: assumes fuller is always better

options.text: That both drafts are accurate, since a commission letter may record an aim as well as a use.
options.misconception: assumes a stated aim is a stated fact

options.text: That the first draft is wrong, since the use of a picture is never part of its record.
options.misconception: ignores the use as evidence

questions.explanation: The first draft stays with what the commission records, while the second adds a claim about what the picture was meant to do. A stated use is evidence; a claimed effect is interpretation.
questions.hint: Ask which draft stays inside the document.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A painter's own account of himself
questions.learningObjective: Weigh a painter's claim by its circumstances
questions.stem: The file on the estate contains a letter in which a painter described his own work as done without help, and the clerk must explain what such a statement is worth.

answer.exemplar: A painter who says he worked alone is making a claim about his standing, and the claim is worth exactly what the circumstances of the letter allow. If it was written to a guild that was pressing him about the quality of a commission, it tells us about the quarrel as much as about the work, and it is still evidence of what he wanted believed at that moment.

questions.explanation: A painter's claim to have worked alone is a claim about his standing, and its weight depends on who was asking and why. It is evidence of what he wanted believed at the time, not a neutral record.
questions.hint: Ask who the letter was written to convince.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Convincing ageing beside modern materials
questions.learningObjective: Count the materials a later varnish explains
questions.stem: A varnish analysis in the file lists three synthetic resins in a painting dated 1610, and a note in the file records that a varnish applied in 1912 contained two of those three resins. How many of the resins found could have come from the 1912 treatment?
questions.explanation: Two of the three resins found are among those in the 1912 varnish, so two could have been introduced by that treatment. The third is not accounted for by that note, though the analysis cannot date it.
questions.hint: Count the resins that the note accounts for.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a school attribution says
questions.learningObjective: Read a workshop label against the visible hand

stimulus.body: A second note in the file describes a painting labelled as by the workshop of a named master. The note records that the panel carries an underdrawing of two figures, that the upper figure was painted over, and that the surviving flesh tones are painted in the manner of the master's documented assistants rather than the master himself.

questions.stem: A second note in the file describes a painting labelled as the work of a master's workshop, and the clerk is asked what the note allows the file to say about the hand.

options.text: That the label may be right, and that the visible work shows the manner of the assistants.
That the painting is a copy, since an assistant's manner cannot appear in a master's workshop at all.
options.misconception: assumes a workshop cannot vary

options.text: That the panel was finished by the master, since the master's style is always present under a later layer.
options.misconception: assumes a hand is fixed by training

options.text: That the overpainted figure shows a later owner altered the picture, since owners do not alter pictures.
options.misconception: reads an alteration as damage by an owner

questions.explanation: A workshop label claims the work was produced inside that workshop, and the assistants' manner is what such a work should show. The overpainted figure shows a change made during the work.
questions.hint: Ask what a workshop label would expect to see.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A label that the handling contradicts
questions.learningObjective: Reason from a mismatch to what follows
questions.stem: The clerk's file asks the surveyor to consider the label on a panel and the handling that contradicts it, and asks for two stages: first to state the contradiction, and then to state what follows.

options.text: State that the handling does not match the label, then say the attribution is open and must be re-examined.
State that the handling does not match the label, then say the signature must be removed from the panel.
options.misconception: assumes a mismatch calls for erasure

options.text: State that the handling does not match the label, then say the panel should be sold as a work of the period.
options.misconception: assumes a mismatch settles a market question

options.text: State that the handling does not match the label, then say the work was painted in a provincial workshop.
options.misconception: assumes a mismatch proves a place

questions.explanation: The first stage states the mismatch as fact, and the second says what follows: the attribution is open and the work needs examining again. A mismatch is not a licence to erase or to price.
questions.hint: Separate what is wrong from what follows.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a workshop contract records
questions.learningObjective: State what a workshop contract shows
questions.stem: A file note records a contract between a master painter and two assistants, and the clerk asks what the document shows about how the pictures were made.

options.text: That a master, assistants and agreed terms existed, and that the work was produced within that arrangement.
That the three men painted each picture together, since a contract binds all of them to every work.
options.misconception: assumes a contract binds every man to every work

options.text: That the assistants were paid by results, since contracts always settled payment by the finished panel.
options.misconception: assumes contracts always pay by results

options.text: That the master chose the subjects, since a contract fixes a price and leaves the subject to the painter.
options.misconception: assumes a contract leaves the subject free

questions.explanation: A contract shows a workshop running on agreed terms between named people, with the work produced inside that arrangement. It does not show who painted which part or chose the subject.
questions.hint: Ask what the document was made to govern.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Patronage and the subject of a picture
questions.learningObjective: Explain how patronage reaches a picture
questions.stem: The clerk's file asks by what route a patron's wishes reach the panel, and the archivist answers in a short statement for the file.

answer.exemplar: A patron's wishes reach a picture through the terms of the commission, through the subject that was paid for, and through the choices the patron made about size, place and material. Beyond that the painter decides how the work is made, and the two kinds of influence are usually easier to separate in the evidence than in the telling, since a contract records terms and a painting records handling.

questions.explanation: Patronage reaches a picture through the terms of the commission, the subject paid for, and the practical choices of size and place. Handling is the painter's own, and the contract tells the two apart.
questions.hint: Ask which decisions the contract records.

questions.stem: A commission letter in the file lists three requirements for a panel, and a note records that the finished panel meets two of them. How many of the stated requirements are unmet?

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A painter's own account of himself
questions.learningObjective: Use a defensive statement as evidence

stimulus.body: A letter in the file describes what the painter said about a picture he was accused of copying: that he had never seen the original, that he had worked from a drawing made by another, and that the picture had been begun before he entered the workshop. The clerk notes that the letter is unsigned and undated.

questions.stem: A letter in the file describes what the painter said about a picture he was accused of copying, and the clerk is asked how the account should be used.

options.text: As a statement made to answer an accusation, which is evidence of what he said and of the quarrel itself.
As proof that the picture is a copy, since a painter never claims to have copied anything.
options.misconception: reads a denial as a confession

options.text: As nothing at all, since the letter is unsigned and undated and therefore cannot be trusted.
options.misconception: rejects a record for want of a signature

options.text: As proof that the workshop was at fault, since only a workshop copies, and painters work alone.
options.misconception: assumes copying is a workshop practice

questions.explanation: A statement made to answer an accusation is evidence of what was said and of the dispute it belonged to. An unsigned letter is a weaker witness, not no witness at all.
questions.hint: Ask what occasion produced the statement.

questions.learningObjective: Reason about imitation and its limits
questions.stem: A question in the file asks how a false surface is made, and the clerk is asked to work in two stages: first to say what a restorer imitates, and then to say what imitation cannot hide.

options.text: Imitate the marks of age, then note that the materials and the handling beneath still give the work away.
Imitate the marks of age, then note that a convincing surface is the last word on the question.
options.misconception: assumes a convincing surface settles a case

options.text: Imitate the marks of age, then note that the age of the picture can be read from the crack pattern alone.
options.misconception: assumes a crack pattern dates a work

options.text: Imitate the marks of age, then note that a restorer may make a work indistinguishable from an original.
options.misconception: assumes imitation cannot be detected

questions.explanation: A restorer imitates the marks of age, and the imitation sits where the evidence of the work should be. Materials and handling lie beneath it, and that is where the test is applied.
questions.hint: Ask what lies beneath the imitation.

questions.learningObjective: State the scope of a workshop label
questions.stem: A file note explains the phrase workshop of the master and the clerk asks what such a phrase lets the file claim about a picture.

That the picture is a copy of a work by the master, since a workshop only repeats what it has seen.
options.misconception: assumes a workshop repeats its master

options.text: That the master designed the picture but never touched it, since a workshop executed only what was drawn.
options.misconception: assumes design and execution are separate

options.text: That the picture is later than the master, since a workshop label is always used for later works.
options.misconception: assumes a workshop label means a later date

questions.explanation: A workshop label claims the work was produced inside that group and by hands other than the master's, and it is a claim about training. It says nothing about copying, design, or date.
questions.hint: Ask whether the phrase names a person or a group.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret a survey of mismatched attributions
questions.stem: A surveyor in the file examines six panels and finds that three of them show handling that does not match the label, and the clerk asks what the survey establishes.

options.text: That half the group disagrees with the label, so the attribution needs revising or the group must be split.
That all six panels are misattributed, since three failures mean the whole group is wrong.
options.misconception: assumes one failure condemns a group

options.text: That the three matching panels are the genuine ones, since a survey tests works one at a time.
options.misconception: assumes a survey settles each work at once

options.text: That the surveyor has made errors, since a label applied to six works cannot be wrong three times.
options.misconception: assumes a label cannot be partly wrong

questions.explanation: Three of six panels inconsistent with the label is a majority, so the attribution needs revising or the group needs splitting. It does not condemn the whole group, nor settle each work.
questions.hint: Ask what a majority of failures allows the file to say.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a workshop contract records
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish fixed terms from open matters
questions.stem: The clerk's file asks which terms a workshop contract fixes, and which it leaves to the painter, and the archivist answers in a short statement.

answer.exemplar: A workshop contract fixes the bargain: the subject or the number of pictures, the dimensions, the price, the materials to be supplied, the dates of payment and the division of labour between master and assistants. It leaves untouched everything that lies behind those terms, namely the handling of the paint, the particular way a head is modelled, and the order in which a panel was actually worked.

questions.explanation: A contract fixes the bargain: subject, size, price, materials, payments and the division of labour. It leaves untouched the handling of the paint and the order of work on the panel.
questions.hint: Ask what a contract was drawn up to settle.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A commission and its stated purpose
questions.learningObjective: Separate a stated purpose from a later use

stimulus.body: A file note records the stated purpose of a commission: the panel was to be set above a chapel altar and to be carried in procession once a year on the feast of the saint. A later entry in the same file records that the panel was sold out of the chapel in 1712 and used as a table top for the next sixty years.

questions.stem: A file note records the stated purpose of a commission and a later sale of the panel, and the clerk is asked what the file may claim about the picture's use.

options.text: That the panel was made for an altar and a procession, and that its later use was a change of function.
That the panel was made for a table, since the use it actually had is the use that counts.
options.misconception: assumes later use settles the making

options.text: That the panel is a copy, since a picture used as a table top cannot have been an altar panel.
options.misconception: assumes later treatment proves a false object

options.text: That the commission was never carried out, since the panel was sold before the year 1712.
options.misconception: assumes a later sale cancels a commission

questions.explanation: The stated purpose and the later use are two separate facts, and a change from altar to furniture is a change of function, not of identity. The commission was carried out, and the file shows both.
questions.hint: Ask whether the two uses are the same fact.

questions.topic: A painter's own account of himself
questions.learningObjective: Set a self-claim against the handling
questions.stem: The clerk's file asks for an account, in two stages, of what a painter's own words can and cannot show, using a letter in which he claimed a picture was entirely his own work.

options.text: Show that he claimed the picture, then keep the claim open and weigh it against the handling of the panel.
Show that he claimed the picture, then treat the claim as proof that no one else touched it.
options.misconception: assumes a claim settles a question of fact

options.text: Show that he claimed the picture, then rule out the work because painters never claim to have worked alone.
options.misconception: assumes a claim is always false

options.text: Show that he claimed the picture, then look for the letter in the estate accounts as the next step.
options.misconception: looks for documents instead of examining the panel

questions.explanation: A painter's claim shows that he made a claim, and the handling of the panel is evidence of another kind that can weigh against it. The claim is the start of the enquiry, not the end of it.
questions.hint: Ask what the claim is evidence of.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Convincing ageing beside modern materials
questions.learningObjective: Weigh surface marks against a label
questions.stem: A label in the file attributes a panel to a named master, and the file notes that the panel carries a fine crack pattern, a brown varnish and a darkened ground, all of which the label describes as age.

options.text: That the described appearance is what a later restorer could produce, so it cannot support the attribution.
That the described appearance proves the panel is a copy, since real age never looks this even.
options.misconception: assumes an even surface proves a false object

options.text: That the described appearance confirms the attribution, since a work of that period must show the same signs.
options.misconception: assumes appearance proves attribution

options.text: That the described appearance dates the panel to the year the varnish was made, since varnish gives a year.
options.misconception: assumes a varnish gives an exact date

questions.explanation: A fine crack pattern, a brown varnish and a darkened ground are marks a restorer can reproduce, so they are not evidence of age by themselves. They need checking against the handling.
questions.hint: Ask what these marks can be imitated by.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a school attribution says
questions.learningObjective: Read the phrase school of in a catalogue
questions.stem: A further note in the file asks for the sense of the term school of as it is used in a catalogue, and the archivist answers in a short statement.

answer.exemplar: School of in a catalogue entry is a deliberate narrowing of the claim, and it says that the work belongs to a group with a shared training while the individual hand is not identified. It is used where the features of the work are strong enough to place it in a group but not strong enough to name a person, and it should be read as a statement about the limits of knowledge rather than a confident attribution.

questions.explanation: School of says the work belongs to a group and does not identify a hand, and it is used where the group is clear but the person is not. It is a statement about the limits of knowledge.
questions.hint: Ask what the phrase narrows down.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A label that the handling contradicts
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the areas without a modern binder
questions.stem: A technical report in the file records that a modern binder was found in the ground of a panel attributed to a sixteenth-century master, and that nine of the fourteen sampled areas showed it. How many of the sampled areas did not show the binder?
questions.explanation: The report samples fourteen areas and finds the binder in nine, so 14 minus 9 areas do not show it. That is 5, and a modern binder in the ground means the surface has been worked on since.
questions.hint: Subtract the areas that showed it from the total.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a workshop contract records
questions.learningObjective: Read a clause as a division of labour

stimulus.body: A file note sets down a contract of 1591 that fixes the subject, the size and the price of two altarpieces, names one assistant to work on both, and provides that the master shall design every part but that the assistant may paint the figures. The note adds that both parties signed, and that the payments were made in three instalments.

questions.stem: A file note sets down a contract of 1591 that fixes the subject, the size and the price of two altarpieces, and the clerk is asked what it shows about how the work was divided.

options.text: That the master designed the work and the assistant painted the figures, with terms settled in advance.
That the assistant painted the whole of both altarpieces, since the contract allows him to paint the figures.
options.misconception: reads a permission as a whole commission

options.text: That the contract was made after the work, since it describes the painting in detail.
options.misconception: assumes a detailed contract follows the work

options.text: That the price was paid in one sum, since contracts of that kind always settled payment at once.
options.misconception: assumes contracts pay in one sum

questions.explanation: A contract naming a design, a task and a price shows labour divided in advance, and permission to paint the figures is a limit as well as a grant. It does not say who touched the rest.
questions.hint: Ask what the clause permits and what it limits.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Patronage and the subject of a picture
questions.learningObjective: Read a list of commissioned subjects together
questions.stem: A patronage note in the file lists the works a guild paid for: an altarpiece with the patron's arms, a banner, and a door panel showing the patron's patron saint.

options.text: That the patron's identity appears in the subjects chosen, which fits a guild buying images of itself.
That the painter chose every subject, since a guild rarely ordered a picture of its own arms.
options.misconception: assumes painters ignore commission terms

options.text: That the works were made for a private house, since public commissions avoided heraldic devices.
options.misconception: reads heraldry as proof of a private setting

options.text: That the banner and the altarpiece are the same work, since a guild paid for one picture in three forms.
options.misconception: assumes one payment means one work

questions.explanation: The subjects carry the patron's arms and the patron's chosen saint, which fits a guild buying images of itself and of what it valued. The list alone does not show who chose each subject.
questions.hint: Ask what the chosen subjects have in common.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A commission and its stated purpose
questions.learningObjective: Weigh a stated purpose against later use
questions.stem: The clerk's file asks whether a stated purpose is evidence of what a picture was actually used for, and the archivist answers in a short statement.

answer.exemplar: A stated purpose is evidence of what the commissioner intended, and intentions are part of a work's history even when the work later found another use. The letter and the account have to be read together, because a panel meant for an altar and then used as a table top is one object with two purposes, and the file should show both rather than choose between them and lose one.

questions.explanation: A stated purpose shows what was intended, and intentions belong to a work's history even when it is later used otherwise. Letter and account are read together, since one object may have had two uses.
questions.hint: Ask whether intention and use are the same thing.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A painter's own account of himself
questions.learningObjective: Use a self-account of training as evidence
questions.stem: A painter's own words in the file describe his early life as spent in a workshop before any independent work, and the clerk asks what the statement can be used for.

options.text: As evidence of a period of training, which helps to explain a shared manner in works of that time.
As proof that he never painted alone, since a painter who trained in a workshop always worked in one.
options.misconception: assumes training fixes a working life

options.text: As proof that the early works belong to his master, since an apprentice cannot own a picture.
options.misconception: assumes an apprentice owns nothing

options.text: As nothing, since a painter's account of his own life cannot be evidence of anything.
options.misconception: dismisses a self-account as worthless

questions.explanation: A statement about a period of training is evidence about the painter's formation, and it helps explain a shared manner in works of that time. It says nothing about how he worked afterwards.
questions.hint: Ask what a period of training can explain.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Convincing ageing beside modern materials
questions.learningObjective: Keep a claim and a finding apart in a file
questions.stem: The clerk's file asks, in two stages, what an artist's account of his own work establishes when the panel in question carries a modern binder in its ground.

options.text: Establish what the painter claimed, then let the material finding stand against the claim separately.
Establish what the painter claimed, then let the material finding settle the question of his honesty.
options.misconception: treats a material finding as a verdict on character

options.text: Establish what the painter claimed, then treat the claim as worthless because it was a letter.
options.misconception: dismisses a written claim entirely

options.text: Establish what the painter claimed to have done, then accept the claim because the panel was later restored.
options.misconception: assumes a later restoration vindicates a maker

questions.explanation: The first stage is what the painter said, and the second is what the materials show. The two belong in the file together, and a material finding settles a date rather than a character.
questions.hint: Keep the statement and the finding apart.

questions.topic: What a school attribution says
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the average share of a group of works
questions.stem: A second attribution in the file distributes thirty works among four named hands within a school, and the clerk asks how many works that works out to for each hand on average.
questions.explanation: Thirty works divided among four hands gives 30 divided by 4, which is 7.5 works per hand on average. An average says nothing about how unevenly the works are actually divided.
questions.hint: Divide the works by the number of hands.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A label that the handling contradicts
questions.learningObjective: Weigh conflicting kinds of evidence

stimulus.body: A surveyor in the file records that the handling of a panel is consistent with the manner of a master in every respect, but that the panel is on a canvas of a weave not used in that region before 1650, and that a carpenter's inscription in the frame reads 1721.

questions.stem: A second surveyor in the file records that the handling of a panel matches a master's manner, but that its canvas and its frame belong to later years, and the clerk is asked what follows.

options.text: That the handling points to the master while the support points elsewhere, so both must be weighed.
That the panel must be a copy, since a work by the master would have been painted on a period canvas.
options.misconception: assumes a support dates the maker

options.text: That the inscription settles the matter, since a dated inscription is stronger than a stylistic opinion.
options.misconception: takes a dated inscription as conclusive

options.text: That the handling is unreliable, since a painter cannot work in a manner after his career ended.
options.misconception: assumes a painter's manner never recurs

questions.explanation: The handling and the support point in different directions, so the file must record both rather than choose. A dated inscription is evidence about the frame, and the manner is evidence about the hand.
questions.hint: Ask which kind of evidence each fact is.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a workshop contract records
questions.learningObjective: Say what a signature does and does not record
questions.stem: The clerk's file asks who signed a workshop contract and what the signature does not record, and asks for two stages: first to say what the signature shows, and then to say what is missing from the record.

options.text: Show that the parties agreed the terms, then say that the actual work on each panel is not recorded.
Show that the parties agreed the terms, then say that the hand which painted the picture is therefore known.
options.misconception: assumes a signature names the hand

options.text: Show that the parties agreed the terms, then say that the price was fixed at the same time as the design.
options.misconception: assumes a contract fixes the design price

options.text: Show that the parties agreed the terms, then say that the contract settles who owned the finished panels.
options.misconception: assumes a contract settles ownership

questions.explanation: A signature shows that named people agreed the terms of a bargain, which is evidence about the workshop. The record does not contain the handling of the paint, and a name is not a hand.
questions.hint: Ask what the document was made to record.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Patronage and the subject of a picture
questions.learningObjective: State what a patron's chosen subject means
questions.stem: A second patronage note in the file states that the subject of a picture was chosen by a patron, and the clerk asks what the note allows the file to claim.

options.text: That the picture was made to present the patron's chosen subject, part of the picture's meaning.
That the picture was made to show the patron's family, since a patron's subject is always a portrait.
options.misconception: assumes a chosen subject is a portrait

options.text: That the painter was paid a large sum, since patrons who choose subjects pay more than others.
options.misconception: assumes a patron's choice implies a large fee

options.text: That the subject was chosen to be flattering, since patrons never choose a subject that embarrasses them.
options.misconception: assumes a patron chooses flattering subjects

questions.explanation: A subject chosen by the patron is part of the picture's meaning, since the work was made to present it and paid for on that understanding. It is not necessarily a portrait.
questions.hint: Ask what the choice of subject tells the file.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A commission and its stated purpose
questions.learningObjective: Set the scope of a commission letter
questions.stem: The clerk's file asks where a commission letter can settle the question of a picture's use, and the archivist answers in a short statement.

answer.exemplar: A commission letter settles the terms on which a picture was made, and the use for which it was intended is one of those terms, so the letter is good evidence of that and of the setting the commissioner had in mind. It is not good evidence of how the picture was handled afterwards, nor of where it hung for centuries, and a file that treats the letter as the end of the story has mistaken an intention for an outcome.

questions.explanation: A commission letter settles the terms, and the intended use is one of them, so the letter is good evidence of that. It is not evidence of how the picture was used or where it hung afterwards.
questions.hint: Ask what the letter was written to agree.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A painter's own account of himself
questions.learningObjective: Read the motive behind a self-claim
questions.stem: A second letter in the file describes the painter's account of himself as the equal of the men he trained beside, and the clerk asks what the tone of the letter shows.

options.text: That the painter was making a case about his standing, which is a motive worth knowing when reading it.
That the painter had in fact trained beside the men he names, since a boast is usually founded in fact.
options.misconception: assumes a boast is founded in fact

options.text: That the letter was written to insult the men named, since equality in this tone is an insult.
options.misconception: reads equality as insult

options.text: That the letter is not by the painter, since painters did not write about their equals in such terms.
options.misconception: judges a document by its manner

questions.explanation: A claim about standing tells the reader the writer had a case to make, and that motive matters when the statement is weighed. It does not settle whether the claim is true.
questions.hint: Ask why the writer would say this.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Convincing ageing beside modern materials
questions.learningObjective: Date separate layers of a panel's surface

stimulus.body: A file note describes a panel whose varnish and craquelure were examined together. The craquelure runs in a uniform network, the varnish is a synthetic resin of a kind not made before 1920, and the paint beneath the varnish shows a fine crack pattern of a quite different size.

questions.stem: A file note describes a panel whose varnish and craquelure were examined together, and the clerk is asked what the findings show.

options.text: That a varnish of the twentieth century and a patterned crack network both postdate the panel's making.
That the panel is a modern fake, since no old work survives a change of varnish.
options.misconception: assumes a later varnish proves a false object

options.text: That the two crack patterns belong to the same hand, since both are fine networks of the same kind.
options.misconception: assumes similar patterns share an origin

options.text: That the panel was painted after 1920, since the varnish is the layer a painter would work on last.
options.misconception: assumes a varnish dates the painting beneath

questions.explanation: A varnish not made before 1920 dates that layer, and a uniform crack network dates the patterned surface, and both postdate the panel. Two crack sizes show two events, not one hand.
questions.hint: Ask what each layer can be dated to.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a school attribution says
questions.learningObjective: Carry a term forward with its sense intact
questions.stem: One note in the file explains the term school of and its use in an earlier catalogue, and the clerk asks what may safely be carried forward.

options.text: The term's sense as a group claim, and the note should say so rather than treat the phrase as a name.
The term's sense as a group claim, and the file should also record it as though the hand were known.
options.misconception: assumes a group claim hides a known hand

options.text: The term's sense as a single painter's name, since catalogues once used it that way.
options.misconception: assumes the term once named a person

options.text: Nothing at all, since an earlier catalogue cannot settle a question about a picture.
options.misconception: dismisses an earlier catalogue as useless

questions.explanation: An earlier catalogue's use of school of shows how the term was being used, and the file should carry forward that sense and no more. The phrase remains a claim about a group and never becomes a name.
questions.hint: Ask what sense the earlier catalogue gives it.

questions.topic: A label that the handling contradicts
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the share of panels a label fails
questions.stem: A survey in the file tests six panels against a label and finds that three contradict it, and the clerk asks what percentage of the panels tested the label does not support.
questions.explanation: Three of the six panels tested contradict the label, so the share is 3 divided by 6. That is 0.5, or 50 per cent of the panels, a finding about the group and not a verdict on one work.
questions.hint: Divide the contradicting panels by the number tested.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a workshop contract records
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a contract's date matters
questions.stem: The clerk's file asks when a workshop contract was made and why the date matters, and the archivist answers in a short statement for the file.

answer.exemplar: The date of a contract matters because it fixes the moment at which the terms were agreed, and that moment governs what the work was meant to be, what materials were expected and who was to be paid. A contract drawn up in 1591 and a copy of it made in 1640 are not the same evidence, and the file has to keep the two apart, because the later copy records what someone believed about the earlier one.

questions.explanation: The date of a contract fixes when the terms were agreed, and it governs what the work was meant to be and who was paid. A contract and a later copy of it are not the same evidence.
questions.hint: Ask what the date fixes and what it cannot.

questions.topic: Patronage and the subject of a picture
questions.learningObjective: Read a patronage note in two stages
questions.stem: A second question in the file asks about a patronage note that lists what a guild paid for, and the clerk is asked to work in two stages: first to state what the note records, and then to say what it leaves open.

options.text: State the works and the payments, then leave open the choices the painter made inside those terms.
State the works and the payments, then treat the choices the painter made inside them as irrelevant.
options.misconception: assumes a commission removes the painter

options.text: State the works and the payments, then conclude that the guild chose every element of each work.
options.misconception: assumes a patron designed every detail

options.text: State the works and the payments, then conclude that the works were made to be sold on the open market.
options.misconception: assumes payment means a market sale

questions.explanation: A patronage note records what was ordered and what was paid, and it leaves open the decisions the painter made. Payment is not a sale to the public, and an order is not a design.
questions.hint: Ask what a payment does and does not record.

questions.topic: A commission and its stated purpose
questions.learningObjective: State what a described purpose allows
questions.stem: A commission description in the file states the purpose of a panel as a gift to a named person, and the clerk asks what the description allows the file to claim.

options.text: That the panel was made to be given, a purpose the file can record and the making can be tested against.
That the panel was painted in the year it was given, since a gift is made for its moment.
options.misconception: assumes a gift dates the work

options.text: That the recipient chose the subject, since a gift begins with the person who receives it.
options.misconception: assumes the receiver chose the subject

options.text: That the panel had no religious purpose, since a gift to a person cannot be devotional.
options.misconception: assumes a gift excludes a devotional use

questions.explanation: A purpose of giving is a fact the file can record and the making can be tested against, since a gift carries expectations of subject and finish. It does not date the work.
questions.hint: Ask what the purpose lets the file test.

questions.topic: A painter's own account of himself
questions.learningObjective: Read a pattern of claims as evidence
questions.stem: A file note lists the claims a painter made in his letters, and counts that he claimed authorship of nine pictures, acknowledged help in three, and denied authorship of one.

options.text: That the pattern of claims is informative, since a man defending his standing leans one way.
That the nine claimed pictures are the genuine ones, since a painter's claims are always true.
options.misconception: assumes a painter's claims are always true

options.text: That the one denied picture is a copy, since a denial is the strongest kind of evidence.
options.misconception: reads a denial as a confession

options.text: That the three acknowledged cases should be removed from the file, since help is not a fault.
options.misconception: assumes an admission removes a work from a record

questions.explanation: The pattern of claims is evidence in itself, since a painter defending his standing will stress one kind of statement and soften another. The counts show how he argued, not which picture is genuine.
questions.hint: Ask what the pattern of claims reveals.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Convincing ageing beside modern materials
questions.learningObjective: Explain where an imitation fails
questions.stem: Convincing an artificial craquelure is the clerk's question, and the archivist answers in a short statement.

answer.exemplar: A well made craquelure can be remarkably convincing, because a network of fine cracks follows the same logic as natural drying and can be placed to follow the tension of the panel. The trouble lies elsewhere, in the places where a natural crack follows a particular event, a knock at the stretcher bar or a movement along a join, and in the layers of dirt and old varnish that a real surface carries and a fresh imitation rarely does.

questions.explanation: A well made craquelure can be convincing, because a network of fine cracks can follow the logic of natural drying. It fails where a real surface shows its history, in cracks that follow events.
questions.hint: Ask where a real surface gives itself away.

questions.explanation: Eighteen works divided among three hands gives 18 divided by 3, which is 6 works per hand on average. The average hides the fact that the hands are credited with very different numbers of pictures.

questions.learningObjective: Separate a support date from a surface date

stimulus.body: A material report in the file finds a modern binder in the ground of a panel attributed to a master of the fifteenth century, and notes that the binder is present over the whole surface, not only in the losses. The report also notes that the panel's oak is dated to 1480 and that the picture is not recorded until 1904.

questions.stem: A material report in the file finds a modern binder in the ground of a fifteenth-century panel, and the clerk is asked what the file may conclude.

options.text: That the panel is old and the surface worked on later, and that the two dates should be kept apart.
That the panel is a modern copy, since a fifteenth-century ground cannot contain a modern binder.
options.misconception: assumes a later material proves a false object

options.text: That the panel was painted in 1904, since that is the first year the picture is recorded.
options.misconception: takes the earliest record as the making

options.text: That the attribution is settled, since the oak is of the right date for the master's career.
options.misconception: assumes a support date settles the hand

questions.explanation: The oak dates the support and the binder dates a surface worked on later, and the picture lies between the panel and the first record. These are separate facts, and a modern binder means later work.
questions.hint: Ask which part of the panel each finding dates.

Show that the parties agreed a sum for named work, then treat the price as a measure of the panels' quality.
options.misconception: assumes a price measures quality

options.text: Show that the parties agreed a sum for named work, then conclude that the assistants were paid the same share.
options.misconception: assumes a price fixes a split

options.text: Show that the parties agreed a sum for named work, then conclude that the contract covered only the materials.
options.misconception: assumes a price covers only materials

questions.explanation: A fixed price shows that the parties agreed a sum for named work, which is real evidence about the bargain. It leaves the handling of the paint open, and says nothing about quality.
questions.hint: Ask what a price fixes and what it cannot.

questions.topic: Patronage and the subject of a picture
questions.learningObjective: State what a commissioned portrait claims
questions.stem: A third patronage note in the file records that the sitter in a portrait paid for by a guild was their secretary, and the clerk asks what the note allows the file to claim.

options.text: That the picture was made to present the guild through its officer, which is a claim about purpose.
That the portrait records the secretary's appearance exactly, since a guild portrait is documentary.
options.misconception: assumes a portrait is a document of appearance

options.text: That the guild chose the sitter without the painter's advice, since a commission names the sitter.
options.misconception: assumes the painter has no part in a likeness

options.text: That the portrait was hung in the guild hall, since a guild pays for pictures it displays.
options.misconception: assumes a payment fixes a location

questions.explanation: A portrait paid for by a guild to show its officer is a statement about the guild as much as the man, and that is a claim about purpose. The commission names the sitter, not the setting.
questions.hint: Ask what the picture was paid to do.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A commission and its stated purpose
questions.learningObjective: Find an inconsistency between two descriptions
questions.stem: Two label drafts in the file are compared for consistency, and the first says the panel was made for a chapel altar, while the second says it was made to be seen in a private house.

options.text: That the two drafts assert different purposes, and that the file has to decide which the evidence supports.
That the first draft is correct, since a chapel is the older and more usual setting for such a panel.
options.misconception: assumes the older setting is the truer one

options.text: That the drafts differ only in wording, since both say the panel was made to be displayed.
options.misconception: assumes similar words mean the same claim

options.text: That the second draft is a correction, since private houses are where such panels usually ended up.
options.misconception: assumes a later setting is the true one

questions.explanation: The two drafts make different claims about purpose, and keeping both without deciding records an argument rather than the work. The evidence has to settle which purpose is supported.
questions.hint: Ask what the two drafts each claim.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A painter's own account of himself
questions.learningObjective: Explain the value of a self-description
questions.stem: The clerk's file asks why a painter's description of himself is evidence at all, and the clerk answers in a short statement.

answer.exemplar: A painter's account of himself is one of the few records made by the person best placed to know the work, and it is written for an audience that will act on it, which is what makes it worth reading. It is also self-interested, partial and sometimes later than the events it describes, and a file that treats it as either a confession or a boast has stopped reading.

questions.explanation: A painter's account is made by the person best placed to know the work and written for an audience that will act on it. It is also partial and self-interested, and both facts belong in the file.
questions.hint: Ask who the account was written for.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Convincing ageing beside modern materials
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the cracks a natural rate would give
questions.stem: A craquelure measurement in the file records that a natural surface cracks about ten times in every ten centimetres, and that the panel in question shows seventy cracks over fifty centimetres. How many cracks would the natural rate have predicted over the same fifty centimetres?
questions.explanation: The natural rate gives ten cracks in ten centimetres, so fifty centimetres would carry 50. The panel shows seventy, well above the natural rate, and that excess is part of what the file records.
questions.hint: Scale the natural rate to the length measured.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a school attribution says
questions.learningObjective: Support a school claim with shared features

stimulus.body: An appendix in the file describes a group of paintings that share a training: the same method of laying a ground, the same shadowing in a transparent brown, and the same narrow range of flesh tones. Three of the group are signed, and their signatures name three different painters, each of whom is documented as having worked in the same city between 1610 and 1630.

questions.stem: An appendix in the file describes a group of paintings that share a training, and the clerk is asked what the note supports.

options.text: That the group was produced in one place and period, and the school label describes that connection fairly.
That the group was painted by one hand, since three painters cannot work in the same manner.
options.misconception: assumes a shared manner means one hand

options.text: That the group was made after 1630, since the dates given only limit the earlier works.
options.misconception: assumes a dated span sets a later date

options.text: That the signatures are forged, since genuine painters do not share a ground and a shadow colour.
options.misconception: assumes a shared style proves false signatures

questions.explanation: A shared ground, shadowing and flesh tones, with the place and dates documented for the signers, support a claim about a shared training in one place and period. A school label describes that fairly.
questions.hint: Ask what the group shares and what the dates add.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A label that the handling contradicts
questions.learningObjective: Record a disputed attribution carefully
questions.stem: The clerk's file asks whose hand a label names when the handling in front of it disagrees, and asks for two stages: first to state the disagreement, and then to state what the file may record.

options.text: State that the handling disagrees with the label, then record an open attribution with the evidence set out.
State that the handling disagrees with the label, then record the attribution as withdrawn from the file.
options.misconception: assumes a mismatch calls for erasure

options.text: State that the handling disagrees with the label, then record the maker as the painter who was working nearby.
options.misconception: assumes a mismatch names a replacement

options.text: State that the handling disagrees with the label, then record the picture as a work of the school instead.
options.misconception: assumes a mismatch produces a broader label

questions.explanation: The first stage states the disagreement between label and handling, and the second records an attribution that is open, with the evidence set out. A disagreement is a reason to look again.
questions.hint: Ask what a disagreement licenses the file to do.
